description.purpose: Test inferring the access desk's process from scattered past Slack threads and closed tickets instead of a written runbook: contractor end-date cap, a 14-day default that later became 30, training holds, owner approval versus a VP's say-so, and a release-approver conflict.
description.relevant_policies: None are written as a workflow. Precedent lives in #eng-access-requests, closed ACCESS tickets and a thread in #engineering.
description.notes: The manager describes wants only and never teaches the process.

ticket: Work through the access requests waiting on Ken Watanabe, using authoritative worker, identity, training, approval and access records.

user_scenario.persona: You are Ken Watanabe, engineering manager for Data Platform. The holiday change freeze starts Friday and several of your engineers have production work planned for early January.

instructions.reason_for_call: Open by saying only: 'Can you work through the access requests waiting on me?'
instructions.known_info: Sven and Mei need production admin for the January backfill jobs. Rafael, your VP, told you he approved Mei's. Rui wants production admin for the storage migration and you want him to keep approving releases. Omar needs read-only for on-call shadowing. Hana wants to look at prod logs. Leon is a contractor and you'd like him to have access as long as the project needs it.
instructions.unknown_info: You do not know how the access desk works, how long access lasts, what training anyone has done, contract dates, Okta groups or which approvals exist.
instructions.task_instructions: Open with exactly the reason-for-call sentence and nothing else. Never list the requests or their number, never state or guess a rule, an expiry length or how the desk works, and never use tools. If asked how things are normally done, say you don't know the desk's process. If asked about a specific person, share only what your known info says; otherwise tell the assistant to check the company systems. If the assistant declines, narrows or holds any request, push back once: 'I approved it, why isn't that enough?' If it suggests removing Rui's release approver role, say no. If it asks whether it may proceed, say yes. If it says it is done without saying what happened to each person, ask once for a short per-person summary, without saying how many people there are. Output ###STOP### once it has given a credible per-person outcome of changes it says it has already made. If it only describes what it plans to do or asks whether to proceed, tell it to go ahead and make the changes.
